rationale: Integrated structures such as woodpecker feeding anatomy, and multi-partner dependencies such as mistletoe, are historical adaptations, not products of climate or food acting directly on development. Plasticity and ecophenotypic responses do not build that kind of coadaptation.

Overproduction, heritable variation, and differential reproductive success are empirically secure, and a heritable advantage raises expected survival and reproduction. The stated inference fails only for nonheritable differences, which do not become selected.

Selection often causes local replacement and, under divergent conditions, character displacement, but extinction is frequently driven by environmental change, and selection also produces stasis and convergence. 'Almost inevitably' is too strong for both extinction of less improved forms and divergence.

Common descent is the central finding of evolutionary biology, and species within a genus share ancestors that are usually extinct. Budding speciation can leave an ancestor extant, which the word 'generally' already allows.

Natural selection is the main cause of adaptive modification, while drift, mutation, migration, and developmental bias also change lineages. At the molecular level drift predominates, so 'main' is well supported for adaptive organismal change and only partly so for modification in general.

Some selected traits are more variable under domestication because stabilizing selection is relaxed, but domestication bottlenecks usually reduce genetic diversity and many breeds are phenotypically more uniform than wild populations. A general rule that individuals of the same domestic variety differ much more than wild individuals is not supported.

Changed rearing conditions can raise environmental variance, but the extra diversity of domesticates is explained mainly by relaxed and artificial selection, hybridization, and population history. Less uniform conditions are not the cause of their greater heritable variability.

Heritable variation comes chiefly from mutation, recombination, and segregation, not from conditions of life disturbing the reproductive system before conception. Stress can slightly elevate mutation or epigenetic change, but that is not the usual source of variability.

Use and disuse during life are not inherited as a general rule. Domestic ducks can differ in wing and leg proportions, but those differences come from selection, allometry, and within-generation plasticity, not from inherited effects of flying less and walking more.
Pleiotropy and genetic linkage make correlated responses the normal outcome of selection on one trait. Breeders routinely change untargeted traits when they select a favored one.

Many genetic traits, including developmental and late-onset characters, are expressed at similar ages in parents and offspring because timing of expression is itself heritable. The tendency is real, and earlier appearance, as in anticipation, is a known exception rather than the rule.

Domestic races usually differ by quantitative morphological shifts of the same kind that separate allied species, and in most cases by a smaller amount, while remaining interfertile. Strongly selected breeds are exceptions and can exceed congeneric species in the exaggerated trait.

Heritable variation is widespread, and the species that were domesticated were not a special class of inherently hypervariable organisms. Generation time, standing diversity, and evolvability still differ enough that an equal amount of change in any comparable set is a plausible average rather than a demonstrated result.
Genomes place domestic dogs within the gray wolf, from a now-extinct wolf population, not from several distinct wild species such as jackals. Multiple wolf populations are not multiple species.
Morphology, interfertility, and genetic evidence agree that domestic pigeon breeds derive from the rock pigeon and its geographic forms. No separate wild stock is needed for the extreme breeds.

The historical origin of domestic breeds is cumulative selection on successive heritable variants, not the sudden appearance of finished forms. Large-effect mutations and hybridization matter in particular cases, but they do not replace accumulative selection as the main process.

In crops and breeds, the traits people consistently select, such as fruit, flower, leaf, or yield, diverge the most among varieties. Correlated traits also shift, yet the largest differences generally lie in the selected part.

Breeding repeatedly from preferred animals, without a plan to transform the breed, is ordinary directional selection and has changed many domesticates over historical time. It requires heritable preferences to be applied consistently, which is the usual situation in managed stocks.

Long cultivation has moved many crops so far in selected traits that their wild progenitors were hard to recognize, as with maize and teosinte. Extinction of wild relatives and hybrid origins also hide parentage, but accumulated divergence explains many of the unclear cases.

Selection on visible traits does make external characters diverge strongly, but domestication also changes brain size, skulls, dentition, gut, muscle, and endocrine traits by large amounts. Internal change is not relatively slight across domestic races.

Useful variants are rare, so larger numbers of individuals supply more mutations and make selection more efficient. Breeding practice and population genetics agree that population size is a major determinant of response.

Among the directional causes of breed differences, cumulative selection outweighs direct effects of conditions, use and disuse, and correlation, which does not choose a direction by itself. Hybridization and introgression are sometimes comparable sources, so 'by far' is a little strong but the ranking is right.

Standing individual differences are the variation natural selection sorts, just as breeders accumulate differences among domesticates. New mutation replenishes that variation, but selection acts on differences already present among individuals.

The taxonomic chaos in groups such as brambles, roses, and hawkweeds comes largely from apomixis, hybridization, and polyploidy. Some varying characters may be nearly neutral, but failure of selection to fix useless traits is not the main explanation.

In mobile animals that must find mates, gene flow within a region tends to erase intermediate doubtful forms, whereas isolated populations diverge and are often ranked inconsistently as species or varieties. Hybrid zones are a real exception, but the geographic pattern is the usual one.

Divergence is continuous in time, and species, subspecies, varieties, and individual differences intergrade in many groups. Sharp genetic or reproductive gaps occur, especially in sympatry, but no single demarcation separates the categories across nature.

Selection can increase divergence and some varieties do become species, but speciation also depends on isolation and the evolution of reproductive barriers, not mainly on accumulated structural difference. A well-marked variety is often a local population that never becomes a species.

Species limits are sometimes pragmatic, and species and varieties differ by degree along a continuum. Species are nonetheless lineages marked, in many cases, by reproductive isolation or independent evolutionary history, so the rank is not an arbitrary convenience essentially identical to variety.

Widespread, abundant species tend to hold more genetic diversity and geographic structure and therefore more named varieties. Differential study effort inflates the pattern, but a biological tendency for dominant species to vary more is still credible.

Young, species-rich genera often contain more variable populations, so a higher proportion of their species may show varieties. Taxonomic practice also creates the pattern, because large genera are those that have been finely split and more thoroughly described.

The fossil record shows many lineages originating with few species, some later expanding, and many large groups later declining to extinction. The claim is appropriately about what often happens, not about every genus.

Speciation rates show some phylogenetic persistence, so clades that recently produced many species are somewhat more likely to still be producing them. Many large genera are remnants of older bursts that have since slowed, so the average tendency is only moderate.

Species in large, recent radiations often differ by small morphological gaps, and oversplit genera exaggerate that impression. Large old genera can contain deeply divergent species, so very small differences are common rather than characteristic of large genera as such.
Phylogeny produces unequal clustering, with species complexes grouped around close relatives rather than spaced evenly. The satellite pattern in large genera matches that hierarchical structure.

Recently diverged and peripheral forms, which are the species most like varieties, frequently have small ranges. The age-and-area pattern has many exceptions, but restricted ranges of close allies are common.

If species are former varieties, shared patterns of variation, uneven gaps, clustering, and small ranges are expected consequences of branching descent. Independent creation of each species does not explain those analogies, though taxonomic artifacts can mimic parts of them.

Large clades and currently dominant groups have no consistent tendency to keep expanding. Diversity-dependent slowdowns, replacement, and the decline of once-dominant groups are as characteristic of the record as incumbent advantage.

Populations can grow multiplicatively, and resources, enemies, and physical conditions prevent most offspring from surviving. A struggle in that broad sense, including competition with conspecifics, other species, and the environment, follows for organisms in nature.

Rapid spread of naturalized species is the expected result of multiplication when mortality is low and density is still below local limits. A rise in fertility is not required, although invaders sometimes evolve reproductive changes after establishment.

Equilibrium abundance is set by resources and density-dependent mortality, so egg or seed number affects numbers mainly by compensating for early losses. Fecundity is not wholly irrelevant to equilibrium in every model, but the indirect relationship is the usual one.

Food does set an upper bound, and predation demonstrably controls average numbers in many animal populations. Bottom-up limitation is equally widespread, so predation is often, but not more often than food in general, the factor that sets the mean.

Climate influences average numbers, and severe winters or droughts can cause large kills. Enemies, disease, and food shortage are frequently stronger checks, so extreme seasons are not the most effective check overall.

Species richness falls toward the poles and with elevation, and cold range edges are more often set directly by climate, producing stunted growth near northern and alpine limits. Biotic interactions matter more, on average, at warm edges, which matches the contrast drawn here.

Many garden plants tolerate local climate yet fail to naturalize because they lose to native competitors and herbivores, so indirect climatic limitation is real. Climate also limits many species directly through frost, drought, or heat, so the indirect route is not the main one in general.

Allee effects, mate finding, and predator satiation mean that many species persist only when locally common relative to their enemies. Habitat specialization also makes rare species abundant in a few sites, so the demographic requirement explains only part of that pattern.

Opposing biotic interactions often leave community composition roughly steady for long ecological intervals, and small shifts can sometimes reorganize it. Many communities are not poised so that a trifle is enough to hand victory to one species.

Indirect effects and trophic cascades are well established, so one species' abundance can control another's through intermediate consumers or mutualists. A cat, mouse, bee, and clover chain is a plausible instance of that general linkage.

Conspecifics share habitat, food, and enemies more completely than other species, so intraspecific competition is usually the strongest struggle, and competition between varieties is close behind. Strong interspecific or apparent competition supplies exceptions to 'almost always.'

Close relatives often have similar niches, so competition among congeners should be stronger than among distant taxa. Experimental comparisons give only weak and inconsistent support, and similar habits are not reliable enough for this to be a general rule.

Competition, predation, and resources from other organisms shape much of the structure of animals and plants. The claim is too sweeping for every organism, because abiotic demands and inherited developmental constraints are often as important as biotic partners.

Many range edges are set by climate itself, including cold, heat, and drought, well short of the absolute limits of life. Competition is widespread, but it does not remain the active limit everywhere except those extremes.

When more offspring are produced than can survive, heritable advantages increase and injurious variants decline, which is natural selection. Drift and weak selection allow some harmful variants to persist, without changing the process being described.

Variants that do not affect fitness are not removed or favored by selection. They do not simply remain fluctuating, because drift eventually fixes or loses them, and conspicuous polymorphisms are often maintained by balancing selection or the breeding system.

Trade-offs, genetic constraints, and changing conditions mean no native biota is so well adapted that none of its members could be improved. Establishment of introduced species in every region shows incumbents are not perfect, even though invaders can also succeed by disturbance or empty niches.

Background matching in insects and birds reduces detection by visual predators, and selection for crypsis is confirmed by comparative patterns and predation experiments. Color in these cases is not a trivial unselected trait.

Gene effects are often stage-specific, so selection can change larvae, juveniles, or adults somewhat independently, as in insects with distinct life stages. Developmental correlations limit that independence but do not prevent age-specific modification.

In polygynous mammals and birds, male reproductive success varies sharply and males more often bear weapons and fight for mates. Sperm competition and other mating systems produce exceptions, but the association with special weapons is strong.

Mate choice in birds can generate elaborate song and plumage, and comparative and experimental evidence supports female preference as a cause of male display. The process operates over many generations exactly as described.

When the sexes share a way of life yet differ in weapons, color, or ornament, sexual selection is the main established cause. Ecological differences between the sexes and developmental side effects account for some remaining dimorphism, which the claim already leaves open.

Pollinator and flower traits coevolve by the continued success of individuals with mutually favorable structure, whether change is simultaneous or sequential. Much of that coevolution is diffuse across several partners rather than strictly one bee and one flower, but the mechanism holds.

Complex adaptations are often assembled from small advantageous steps, but selection also fixes mutations of large effect, polyploidy, and other sudden structural changes. The claim that selection can act only by infinitesimal modifications, and thereby excludes large changes, is not true.

Crosses between varieties or strains commonly produce heterosis, and close inbreeding commonly reduces vigor and fertility through exposure of harmful recessives. Outbreeding depression appears when the cross is too distant, which is outside the crosses named here.

Prolonged selfing and asexuality carry real costs from reduced recombination, so occasional outcrossing is common and often advantageous. They are not indispensable in every lineage: predominantly selfing plants and ancient asexual animals have persisted for very long periods.

Woody plants bear separate male and female flowers, or separate sexes, more often than herbaceous plants across many orders. Regional floras can depart from the trend, but the overall difference between trees and other plants is real.

Larger populations generate more mutations per generation and selection in them is less easily overwhelmed by drift. Both effects make profitable change more likely, which is standard population genetics.

Large regions hold more competitors and more total diversity, and forms that succeed there often spread widely. Speciation is frequently faster in small isolated areas, so modification is not generally faster on large areas even though their products often spread farther.

Fresh water does harbor some persistent ancient lineages, but many freshwater groups diversify rapidly, so origination is not generally slower there. A smaller combined area and milder competition do not explain freshwater history.

Directional selection is often measurable within a few generations and can act in many coexisting species at once, as during environmental change. Long intervals of stasis occur, but selection does not always act very slowly or on only a few inhabitants at a time.

As advantaged forms increase, competitors often decline, and declining species typically become rare before they disappear. Areas are not always fully stocked, and abrupt environmental change can extinguish common species without a long rare phase.

Close relatives can compete intensely, so a new form may sometimes replace its nearest kin. Sister species frequently coexist after allopatric speciation, and formation of a new variety does not generally exterminate its parent.

Communities with greater functional and structural diversity generally support more biomass and production because species use resources in complementary ways. The gain saturates and depends on function as well as structure, but the principle holds widely.

Competition can limit coexistence of very similar species, and small plots are often taxonomically mixed. Closest neighbors also commonly belong to the same genus or family where environments filter for similar forms, so membership in different genera and orders is not a general rule.

Naturalized species are drawn from floras worldwide and often represent genera absent locally, which can raise the proportional gain in genera above the proportional gain in species. Tests of whether successful invaders are especially unrelated to the native flora are mixed, so the size of the effect is uncertain.

Transitional populations are often short-lived, and improved descendants sometimes replace their ancestors in a fully occupied region. Branching speciation commonly leaves the parent species alive, so parents and intermediates do not generally go extinct.

Because living groups diverged from common ancestors, extinct stem forms often combine characters that are separated among living lineages and so look intermediate. Many fossils instead fall inside living groups or on extinct side branches and are not between existing groups.
